report:
I now have strong, consistent evidence from multiple systematic reviews/meta-analyses of RCTs. Here's my report.

## Report: Does offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) increase HIV testing uptake?

**Yes — the evidence strongly supports this conclusion.** Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) consistently show that offering HIVST, in addition to or instead of standard facility-based testing, significantly increases the proportion of people who test for HIV.

A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs among key populations (men who have sex with men, sex workers, transgender people, etc.) found that distributing free HIVST kits increased testing uptake compared to standard-of-care testing overall and across all subgroups analyzed (link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z).

A companion 2021 review in *EClinicalMedicine*, updating earlier evidence that informed the WHO's 2016 recommendation for HIVST, similarly confirmed higher testing uptake with self-testing versus standard services (thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext).

In sub-Saharan Africa specifically, a 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis (PLOS ONE) examining effects among general adult populations found that HIVST significantly increased uptake of HIV testing, though effects on downstream linkage to antiretroviral treatment were more mixed (journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0245498).

Large-scale programmatic evidence from the HIV Self-Testing Africa (STAR) Initiative — cluster-randomized evaluations across Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe — reinforced these trial findings, demonstrating that community-based lay distribution of self-test kits increased testing coverage, notably reaching men, adolescents, and first-time testers who were otherwise underserved by conventional testing services (menstarcoalition.org/undiagnosed/hiv-self-testing-africa-initiative-star/).

**Caveat:** while uptake reliably increases, some reviews note this doesn't always translate into a proportional rise in new HIV diagnoses or successful linkage to care — an important consideration for full public health impact, though it doesn't undermine the core finding about testing uptake itself.
